title: US Senator Introduces Bill to Freeze H-1B Visas for Three Years
excerpt: Senator Tim Sheehy's End H-1B Abuse Act would halt new H-1B issuance, codify a $100,000 petition fee, and restart the program with a 25,000 annual cap and $200,000 minimum salary.
body:
• Senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) introduced the End H-1B Abuse Act, seeking a three-year pause on new H-1B visas
  • The bill would slash the annual cap from 65,000 to 25,000 and set a minimum salary of $200,000 per year when the program restarts
  • It would codify President Trump's proposed $100,000 fee per H-1B petition, which was struck down by a federal court
  • The legislation follows a similar House bill introduced by Rep. Eli Crane in April with eight Republican co-sponsors

The Senate Bill

Republican Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana introduced the End H-1B Abuse Act of 2026 on Thursday, proposing to suspend all new H-1B visa issuance for three years before restarting the program under far stricter rules, The Hindu Business Line reported.

"The H-1B program was created to address workforce shortages for specialized, difficult-to-fill positions — not to displace qualified, hardworking Americans with cheaper, foreign labor."

— Senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana)

The bill would also codify the $100,000 fee per H-1B petition that the Trump administration had imposed but which was struck down by a federal court. It is backed by the Immigration Accountability Project and the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR).

Sweeping Restrictions

When the program resumes after the three-year freeze, the bill envisions a radically different H-1B system. The annual cap would drop from 65,000 to 25,000, with existing exemptions eliminated. The current lottery would be replaced with a wage-based selection system, and the minimum salary for H-1B positions would rise to $200,000 per year.

Additional provisions would bar H-1B workers from holding multiple jobs, prohibit third-party staffing agencies from employing them, end the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program for international students, and prevent visa holders from bringing dependents to the United States.

The bill would also prohibit H-1B holders from adjusting their status to permanent residency, requiring them to leave the country before changing to another nonimmigrant status — effectively eliminating the program as a pathway to a green card.

Building on House Legislation

Sheehy's Senate bill follows a companion House measure introduced by Representative Eli Crane (R-Arizona) in April, with co-sponsors including Representatives Brian Babin, Brandon Gill, Wesley Hunt, Keith Self (all Texas), Paul Gosar (Arizona), Andy Ogles (Tennessee), and Tom McClintock (California).

"The federal government should work for hardworking citizens, not the profit margins of massive corporations."

— Representative Eli Crane (R-Arizona)

The House bill contained similar provisions, with American Bazaar Online reporting that existing visa holders would be required to wind down their stay during the pause period. Under the proposal, H-1B stays would be capped at a single three-year term with no extensions.

Impact on Indian Workers

Indian professionals form one of the largest groups of H-1B visa holders, with tens of thousands employed across American technology companies each year. The proposed legislation would hit Indian tech workers and their families particularly hard — the ban on dependents would affect spouses on H-4 visas, and ending the OPT program would remove a critical bridge for Indian students transitioning from U.S. universities to the workforce.

The $200,000 minimum salary would put the threshold well above what many entry-level and mid-career tech positions currently pay, potentially pricing out a significant portion of the Indian workforce that the H-1B program currently serves.

While the bill faces long odds in a divided Congress, its introduction in both chambers signals that H-1B restrictions remain a priority for a vocal bloc of Republican lawmakers — keeping the issue front and center as Indian professionals and students plan their careers around the U.S. immigration system.
